title: Tools and MCPs
intro: This domain covers how Claude reaches beyond text generation: implementing tools (function calling, schemas, descriptions, error handling, client-side versus server-side execution, approval patterns), developing MCP servers (tools, resources, prompts, and the stdio versus network transport decision), and — the judgment layer — choosing among built-in tools, custom tools, Skills, and MCPs for a given use case. Exam questions reward candidates who treat tool definitions as an interface contract and who can articulate why a requirement points at one extension mechanism rather than another.

objectives.explanation:
Function calling works on a simple contract: you send tool definitions (name, description, JSON schema for parameters) with the request; the model decides when a tool applies and responds with a structured tool-use request; your code executes the tool and returns the result; the model continues with that result in context. The model never executes anything itself — it emits intentions your harness dispatches. That makes the definitions the entire interface: the model selects tools and constructs arguments purely from names, descriptions, and schemas. Descriptions should read like good API documentation — what the tool does, when to use it (and when to use a sibling tool instead), what each parameter means with formats and examples, and what comes back. Most wrong-tool and malformed-argument failures are documentation failures, fixable without touching architecture.

Execution location and governance are design decisions. Client-side tools run in your application, giving you full control over implementation, credentials, and environment; server-side tools execute on Anthropic's infrastructure. Approval patterns should be risk-proportional: read-only, reversible operations run automatically; consequential actions — payments, deletions, external communications — pause for human confirmation before execution. In agentic harnesses, the dispatch loop plus permission checks and hooks form the governance layer around every call.

Because arguments are model-constructed, tools must treat them as untrusted input: validate existence, formats, ranges, and the caller's authorization server-side before any state-changing operation. And error handling is part of the interface — the tool result is the model's only feedback channel, so failures should return as structured, descriptive, actionable messages ('invoice INV-993 not found; verify via search_invoices'), never as loop-killing exceptions or, worse, false success. Tool-set construction rounds it out: a handful of focused, well-named, non-overlapping tools beats a sprawl of ambiguous ones competing for the model's attention.
objectives.whyItMatters: Tools are where the model touches real systems, so tool quality is application quality: vague descriptions produce wrong calls, unvalidated arguments produce wrong writes, and brittle error handling turns recoverable hiccups into dead agent loops. Teams routinely find that rewriting tool descriptions fixes 'model reliability' problems no prompt tweak could.

examples.title: Fixing tool misuse with documentation, not architecture
examples.body: A logistics agent with search_shipments ('Searches shipments') and get_shipment_details ('Gets details') keeps calling the wrong tool and passing tracking numbers where internal IDs belong. The rewrite makes each definition self-sufficient: search_shipments — 'Find shipments by customer name, route, or date range; returns summaries with shipment_id. Use when you don't yet have a shipment_id.' get_shipment_details — 'Fetch one shipment's full record. Requires shipment_id (format SHP-XXXXXX, from search results); tracking numbers are not accepted.' Parameter descriptions gain formats and examples. Wrong-tool calls and guessed parameters drop sharply — the model finally has the documentation it was implicitly being asked to imagine.

examples.title: A billing tool that fails safely and honestly
examples.body: An invoice-adjustment tool called by an agent initially crashes the loop on unexpected input and once adjusted a nonexistent invoice ID that parsed as valid. Hardened, the tool validates before acting — the invoice exists, the amount is within policy range, the requesting session is authorized for that account — and returns failures as structured results: {"error": "invoice_not_found", "message": "INV-993 does not exist; use search_invoices to verify the ID"}. Adjustments above a threshold additionally require human approval before execution. The agent now recovers from bad IDs in one iteration, and no state change happens on unvalidated arguments.

pitfalls: One-line tool descriptions — the model selects tools and builds arguments from descriptions and schemas alone; underdocumented tools guarantee wrong calls.
Trusting model-constructed arguments — they are untrusted input; validate existence, format, range, and authorization server-side before any state change.
Letting tool exceptions kill the agent loop, or returning false success to keep it smooth — return structured, actionable error results; honest failure is recoverable, false success compounds.
Uniform approval policies — gating every read destroys responsiveness while consequential actions deserve the review; make approval proportional to risk and reversibility.
Tool sprawl with overlapping responsibilities — many vaguely differentiated tools degrade selection; prefer a small set of focused, clearly bounded tools.

objectives.explanation:
The Model Context Protocol standardizes how AI applications connect to external capabilities: instead of every app hand-wiring every integration, an MCP server exposes capabilities once and any MCP client — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, or your own application — connects to it. A server offers three capability types: tools (model-invoked operations with schemas, the workhorse), resources (data the client can read into context — files, records, query results), and prompts (reusable, parameterized prompt templates the server provides). Authoring a server with the official SDKs is mostly decorating functions with names, descriptions, and typed parameters — the same documentation discipline as tool implementation, because the model consumes these definitions the same way.

Transport is the key deployment decision, and it follows topology. stdio transport: the client launches the server as a local subprocess and communicates over stdin/stdout — simple, no network surface, ideal for personal and local integrations like a server on each developer's laptop serving Claude Desktop or Claude Code. Network transports (streamable HTTP): the server runs as a standing service that many clients reach over the network — right for shared, team- or organization-wide capabilities, and the point where authentication, authorization, and access control become the server's responsibility. Capabilities are transport-independent: the same tools, resources, and prompts travel over either; transport is a property of the connection, not of individual tools.

Integration is configuration on the client side: register the server (command to launch for stdio, URL for network) and its capabilities appear to the model alongside native tools. Operationally, treat a shared MCP server like any service — version it, log tool invocations, scope credentials to what its tools genuinely need, and remember that a server used by many applications concentrates both value and risk: its bugs, and its permissions, are inherited by every client.
objectives.whyItMatters: MCP is the ecosystem's answer to the N-apps-times-M-integrations explosion — build the integration once, connect it everywhere, version it independently. Developers who confuse the transports ship local prototypes that can't be shared, or expose unauthenticated network servers that any client can drive.

examples.title: One server, two transports, two audiences
examples.body: A genomics platform team builds an MCP server for sample-tracking: tools for querying samples and booking sequencer time, resources exposing run manifests. Scientists use Claude Desktop on managed laptops, so their configuration launches the server locally via stdio — a subprocess per user, no network surface, lab credentials stay on the machine. The cloud analytics agents instead connect to a deployed instance of the same server over streamable HTTP behind the company's identity-aware proxy, with per-service credentials. Same codebase and capability set; the transport — and its security posture — follows where each client runs.

pitfalls: Choosing a network transport for a purely local, single-user integration — stdio is simpler and exposes no network surface; save HTTP for genuinely shared servers.
Exposing a network-reachable MCP server without authentication — a reachable server is drivable by any client; auth and access control are mandatory the moment you leave stdio.
Treating everything as a tool — data that should simply be readable belongs in resources, and reusable prompt patterns in prompts; using the right capability type keeps servers legible.
Writing thin tool descriptions because 'it's just our server' — MCP tools are consumed by the model exactly like native tools; the documentation bar is identical.
Forgetting that a shared server's permissions are inherited by every connected client — scope its credentials tightly; it is a concentration point for risk as well as reuse.

objectives.explanation:
Claude can be extended four ways, and choosing among them is a recurring design decision. Built-in tools are capabilities the platform already provides (file operations, shell, web access in supporting products) — zero build cost, but fixed scope: they cannot know your internal systems or contracts. Custom tools are functions you define in one application via function calling — the lightest path to app-specific behavior, owned by that app, but private to it: a second app means a second implementation. Skills are packaged procedural knowledge — instructions, templates, conventions, optionally supporting scripts and resources — that Claude loads when a matching task arises; they teach how to do something the company way. MCP servers expose executable capabilities as a standalone, independently owned and versioned service that any number of Claude applications connect to.

Two questions cut through most cases. First: does Claude need to know something or reach something? Procedural knowledge — report formats, review checklists, house workflows — is a Skill; live access to systems and data is a tool or MCP server. Infrastructure is the wrong container for knowledge (an MCP server whose tools return procedure text is overhead with no integration), and knowledge is the wrong container for integration (a Skill full of curl examples leaves every app improvising unauthenticated calls). Second, for executable capabilities: what is the scope of reuse and ownership? One application, one team — a custom tool suffices. Many applications, or a platform team that wants to own and version the integration independently of consumers — that is MCP's design case.

Costs scale with the choice: built-in < Skill ≈ custom tool < MCP server in build-and-operate burden, so prefer the lightest mechanism that meets the actual reuse, ownership, and access requirements — and combine them freely: an agent might use built-in file tools, a Skill for the workflow, and an MCP server for the live data behind it.
objectives.whyItMatters: Teams that misjudge this build MCP infrastructure for single-app needs, copy-paste custom tools across five codebases that drift apart, or stuff live-integration jobs into Skills that can't authenticate. The extension mechanism decides who maintains the capability, how it's shared, and what breaks when the underlying system changes.

examples.title: Know something vs. reach something
examples.body: An insurance carrier has two requests the same week. Actuarial wants Claude Code to produce reports 'the company way' — a documented multi-step procedure, data-validation rules, a mandated structure, house terminology, and a Python rendering script; nothing external to touch. That is packaged procedural knowledge: a Skill bundling the instructions, template, and script, loaded when report tasks arise. Platform engineering wants five Claude applications to query live machine telemetry and schedule maintenance, with the integration owned and versioned by one team. That is shared executable capability: an MCP server exposing the operations as tools, each app a client. Swapping the mechanisms — a telemetry Skill of curl examples, or an MCP server serving procedure text — would fail both teams.

examples.title: Escalating from custom tool to MCP
examples.body: A retail team ships a single Claude app with a custom get_inventory tool — twenty lines against the warehouse API, perfect for the job. Six months later three more teams want inventory access and have started copying the function; the schemas have already drifted, and a warehouse API change now means four coordinated fixes. The platform group extracts the integration into an MCP server owned by the warehouse team: one schema, one credential policy, one place to absorb API changes, and new applications connect by configuration. The initial custom tool was the right call for one app; the migration point arrived exactly when reuse and ownership requirements changed.

pitfalls: Standing up an MCP server for a single-application need — if one app owns and uses the capability, a custom tool delivers the same result without transport, deployment, and configuration overhead.

Distributing procedural knowledge as infrastructure — procedures, templates, and conventions are Skill content; servers whose tools return static instruction text are overhead pretending to be integration.
Packaging live-system access as a Skill — docs-plus-examples leaves every consumer improvising calls with no typed schema or managed credentials; executable access wants a tool or MCP server.
Copy-pasting custom tools across applications — parallel implementations drift and multiply maintenance; recurring cross-app reuse is the signal to extract an MCP server.
Assuming built-in tools cover internal systems — built-ins provide general capabilities; authenticated, structured access to your own platforms requires custom tools or MCP.
